restaurant_name: Queen Sirikit National Institute of Child Health
text:
Review of the most recent visit, 01/04/2015. This time, my child suffered a wound from a slip and fall accident.
- 8:00 PM: Went to the front of the Siam Building on the second floor. A nurse screened me, asked about my symptoms, and met with a surgeon. After assessing my wound, I was admitted to the hospital. I didn't have to wait long for a room that night.
- My child was in a private room. The nurses were lovely and very helpful. The room was nice and comfortable, with a sofa bed. During my visit, a few days after the earthquake, the hospital kitchen was closed, so the food was boxed like at 7-Eleven.
- The doctor came in the morning and evening, assessed my symptoms, and then gave me medication and warm water. All the doctors were lovely and very polite. They were kind to the children. After two nights, they were able to go home.
- Two other great things were that a NHSO official came to talk to me and provide advice about the Gold Card scheme. A psychiatrist also came to talk to parents about concerns about their children or the accident.
- Gold Card members receive discounts on doctor and medication fees at the hospital under their coverage. My child was at another hospital, but since it was an emergency, they were able to use their benefits.
- The parking lot at the Chalerm Prakiat Building was closed due to the earthquake. The hospital has a food court. 7-Eleven and food vendors.
- Overall, I was very impressed with the service I received this time. Personally, I've never had a bad experience. However, I understand that public hospitals are crowded with patients and staff are few, so it can be slow, with long waits and sometimes rude staff. However, the doctors are excellent and the medicine and medical fees are reasonable. I feel reassured that there's a good children's hospital when my child is sick.

restaurant_name: Queen Sirikit National Institute of Child Health
text: We took our child to get treatment for a vascular tumor. We waited in line until a nurse called our child's name. We went to the nurse and asked if we could see a medical student, but said that a senior doctor would also examine the child first. We hesitated, not knowing how to respond, because we wanted to see the senior doctor directly. The nurse then said that if we didn't see a medical student, they wouldn't issue us another appointment. So we reluctantly agreed. In short, the medical student knew nothing about our child's condition. They just asked basic questions and didn't do any examinations. When we went to see the senior doctor, it was even worse. After examining the child, they said, "Oh, it will go away on its own," and didn't issue another appointment. They didn't explain anything to us at all, even though we traveled four hours by car to see this doctor.

restaurant_name: Queen Sirikit National Institute of Child Health
text:
I was referred here for treatment. Dr. J. has been terrible since I started receiving treatment here.
My mental health has deteriorated. My child was already sick, and then this doctor started intimidating and threatening me. It was incredibly cruel, having to endure waiting for my child to be treated by him. Even now, I still feel scared—afraid of his shouting, afraid of him pointing his finger, afraid of his cursing. I've been very patient, never retaliating, never asking why he speaks like that. I never want to go back because I'm afraid of him. He points at me and tells me to look him in the face! He says, "Look me in the eyes!" He slams the table. "I know what kind of person you are, Mom." I don't understand how he knows what kind of person I am. And he shouts at the top of his lungs, his words echoing outside the room. There were four assistants, and none of them dared to say anything. My child contracted an infection after surgery, a Kawasaki disease. We were moved from the 6th floor of the surgical ward to the 8th floor, and he still came up to curse at us.
Even when my child was asleep, he yelled at me not to use my phone. At that time, I had to sell things because I had household expenses and school fees for three other children. No one came to visit or rotate shifts for months, and I was already very stressed. Why did he treat me like this? Why wouldn't I be allowed to use my phone? We sell goods in our neighborhood, and my boyfriend has them delivered. We have to order and pay for the goods we sell. We sell coconuts to a large stall at Wat Luang Pho To. This doctor had a nurse hang a sign on a cardboard box with writing in marker saying "No mobile phones allowed in this bed." He said our child has ADHD and is autistic, but we didn't let our child use a phone. Our child is perfectly normal; we've had developmental pediatricians say everything is normal. But he wouldn't let me use a phone either. It's a matter of personal privacy, isn't it? We couldn't say anything. If we tried to speak, he would point at us, and we were terrified. He said he was the one who accepted our child's case. We didn't dare say anything during our hospital stay, which lasted for many months—7 months in total. We hardly ever slept at home. When we came back, we would have stomach pain and need to go back to the hospital. Life there was incredibly difficult. We suffered mentally and emotionally, crying every day because we were taking care of our child alone. We want our mental health to improve because we're still afraid and don't dare go back for treatment.
#But I want to thank you for helping with the surgery that relieved my child's stomach pain. I truly appreciate it from the bottom of my heart. But I still don't dare go back to see the doctor again.
